chunks.text: Long ago, King Janaka welcomed the wise sage Vishwamitra and two princes, Rama and Lakshmana, to his kingdom one bright morning. He bowed to the sage and asked what he could do for him. Vishwamitra said the two princes wished to see the great bow that Janaka kept, and asked him to show it to them.

Janaka told them the story of the bow. Long ago it belonged to the god Shiva, who had once been angry with the gods and threatened them with it. The gods prayed to Shiva, and he was pleased and gave the bow to them, and it was passed down as a trust until it came to Janaka's family.

Janaka also told them about his daughter, Sita. Once, while he was ploughing a field for a sacrifice, he found a girl who had risen from the earth, and she grew up as his own daughter. Janaka decided that only someone who could bend his great bow would be allowed to marry Sita. Many kings had come and tried, but not one of them could even lift the bow, so Janaka sent them all away.

Angry at this, some kings attacked his city, Mithila, for a whole year, until Janaka prayed to the gods for help. The gods gave him a great army, and the attacking kings were driven away. Now, Janaka said, he would let Rama try to string the bow, and if he could, Sita would become his wife.

So Janaka ordered his ministers to bring out the bow. It was so heavy that it lay in an iron box on a huge cart with eight wheels, and five thousand strong men had to pull it. Janaka told everyone that not even gods or great spirits had ever been able to string this bow.

Then Rama stepped forward and opened the case. He asked if he might touch the bow and try to bend it, and Janaka and Vishwamitra told him to go ahead. In front of a huge crowd, Rama picked up the bow easily, fixed the string, and pulled it back. With a sound like a thunderclap, the great bow snapped in two! The noise was so loud that the ground shook, and everyone in the crowd fell over except for Janaka, Vishwamitra, Rama, and Lakshmana.

When everyone had calmed down, Janaka joined his hands together and told Vishwamitra that he could hardly believe what he had just seen. He said his daughter Sita would now marry Rama, just as he had promised. Janaka happily sent messengers riding to Ayodhya to bring King Dasaratha the wonderful news, and to invite him to come to Mithila.
